title: Bloom's Taxonomy of Educational Objectives, Center for the Advancement of Teaching Excellence, University of Illinois Chicago
text: Bloom's Taxonomy, originally published in 1956, was revised by Anderson and Krathwohl in 2001, and this revised version is the one commonly used today. The most visible change was converting the categories from nouns into action verbs, so learning objectives describe what a learner does. The revised model articulates six cognitive process levels arranged from foundational to higher-order thinking: Remember (retrieving relevant knowledge from memory), Understand (determining the meaning of instructional messages), Apply (using procedures in given situations), Analyze (breaking material into components to understand relationships), Evaluate (making judgments based on criteria and standards), and Create (producing new or original work). Instructional designers use this progression to scaffold learning experiences that build progressively more complex cognitive demands, choosing measurable verbs that match the intended level. The 2001 revision also introduced a second axis called the Knowledge Dimension, turning the taxonomy into a two-dimensional matrix. The Knowledge Dimension comprises four categories: Factual knowledge (the basic elements of a discipline), Conceptual knowledge (the relationships between elements within a larger structure), Procedural knowledge (methods, techniques, and how to do something within a discipline), and Metacognitive knowledge (awareness and understanding of one's own cognition and how learning functions relative to oneself). Metacognitive knowledge was a genuinely new addition in the revision. By crossing the six cognitive processes with the four knowledge types, designers can specify both what kind of thinking and what kind of knowledge an objective targets, producing more precise and intentional course design. Although the six processes are ordered, their boundaries are not rigid and often overlap in practice.

title: Action Mapping and xAPI (Cathy Moore's method), xAPI.com
text: Action mapping is a learning design process developed by Cathy Moore in 2008. It challenges the common practice of designing training as an information dump by insisting that design start from a measurable business goal rather than from content, and by first asking whether training is even the right solution. The process moves backward from outcomes to knowledge through four sequential steps: first, identify the business goal; second, identify what people need to do on the job to reach that goal; third, design activities that let people practice each of those behaviors; and fourth, identify the minimum information people need to complete each activity. Working in this reverse order prevents the usual trap of building content-centered courses whose relevance to actual performance is never examined. Action mapping prioritizes behavior change over information delivery, so the activities it produces tend to be practical and realistic, often mirroring the decisions and tasks of the real job rather than abstract quizzes. Only after the required behaviors and practice activities are clear does the designer add the smallest amount of supporting information needed, keeping materials focused on improving performance. Moore frames the aim as changing what people do, not just what they know. The method gains further power when paired with measurement: pilot projects instrumented with xAPI can test whether the identified behaviors and information actually move the business goal before a full organizational rollout, replacing assumptions with evidence of impact.

title: Mayer's 12 Principles of Multimedia Learning, Digital Learning Institute
text: Richard Mayer's cognitive theory of multimedia learning rests on three assumptions about how people process information: the dual-channel assumption (auditory and visual content are processed through separate pathways), the limited-capacity assumption (each channel can handle only a finite amount at once), and the active-processing assumption (learners benefit most when they engage meaningfully rather than passively receive content). From this theory Mayer derived twelve design principles. The multimedia principle holds that people learn better from words and pictures together than from words alone. The coherence principle recommends excluding extraneous material that distracts from the core objective. The signaling principle advises highlighting essential information through cues such as arrows, headings, or bold text. The redundancy principle warns against presenting the same information as narration plus identical on-screen text, which overloads a channel. The spatial contiguity principle says to place related words and visuals near each other, and the temporal contiguity principle says to present corresponding words and pictures at the same time rather than in sequence. The segmenting principle calls for breaking complex material into learner-paced chunks, and the pre-training principle suggests teaching key names and concepts before the full lesson. The modality principle favors graphics with spoken narration over graphics with on-screen text. The personalization principle recommends conversational rather than formal language, the voice principle finds human narration outperforms machine-generated speech, and the image principle notes that a static talking-head image of the instructor does not necessarily improve learning. Together these principles help designers manage extraneous, essential, and generative processing so multimedia instruction reduces cognitive overload.

title: The Audio Producer's Guide To Loudness, Transom.org (Rob Byers / Jeff Towne)
text: LUFS (Loudness Units Full Scale, also written LKFS) is the primary unit for measuring perceived loudness in modern audio production. Unlike peak meters that measure electrical level in dBFS, LUFS applies K-weighting to account for the frequency sensitivity and duration characteristics of human hearing, so it tracks how loud something actually sounds. One Loudness Unit (LU) is a perceptually noticeable step, so -20 LUFS is 4 LU louder than -24 LUFS. The recommended production standard is -24 LUFS, which aligns with the ATSC A/85 standard (established under the CALM Act for television) and the Public Radio Satellite System loudness standard. Targeting -24 LUFS leaves adequate headroom for voice storytelling, roughly 6 dB of space before clipping, without forcing heavy compression or limiting. For podcast distribution the mix may then be raised to about -18 or -16 LUFS, though pushing that far usually requires a compressor during production. Loudness is measured over different windows: Short Term uses a rolling 3-second window and is useful for judging balance while mixing, while Integrated loudness averages the entire piece and predicts episode-to-episode consistency but must be computed over the whole program. True Peak, measured in dBTP, uses oversampling to catch inter-sample peaks that ordinary peak meters miss and appears in delivery specs such as -24 LUFS with peaks no higher than -1 dBTP. Loudness normalization shifts an entire file up or down to hit a target integrated loudness, preserving the relative balance between elements and keeping episodes consistent, but it cannot fix internal balance problems and can trigger limiter artifacts when managing peaks.

title: Podcasting Basics, Part 5: Loudness for Podcasts vs. Radio, Transom.org
text: Radio and podcasts call for two different loudness targets. Traditional public radio aims for -24 LUFS (Loudness Units relative to Full Scale), while podcasts target roughly -18 LUFS. The Audio Engineering Society recommends that talk-format podcasts center on -18 LUFS, which sits in the middle of a recommended range of -20 to -16 LUFS depending on content style. The difference reflects distinct playback environments. Radio's lower -24 LUFS standard preserves dynamic range, letting producers keep varied peaks while holding a consistent average, which suits music and traditional broadcast programming that stations further process before transmission. Podcasts need the higher -18 LUFS target because mobile devices have limited amplification and listeners often consume episodes in noisy settings such as commuting, driving, or doing chores. As the article puts it, louder listening environments combined with a mobile device's inability to pump up the volume mean a higher loudness target is needed for podcasts. The recommended practical workflow is to mix content at the lower -24 LUFS radio standard regardless of the final destination, then convert to -18 LUFS by limiting peaks to create headroom and raising the overall gain. Working this way avoids the distortion that results from trying to record or mix directly at the higher podcast level, and it keeps a single clean master that can be delivered to either radio or podcast at the appropriate level.

title: What Are LUFS? The Complete Guide, iZotope Learn
text: LUFS stands for Loudness Units Full Scale and measures perceived loudness rather than simple amplitude. Loudness units are the same size as decibels, but they factor in how the ear and brain interpret loudness based on a sound's tonal balance. This is achieved with K-weighting, a filter that applies a 4 dB high-shelf boost above 2 kHz plus a high-pass filter around 100 Hz to simulate human hearing sensitivity. A LUFS meter reports several metrics. Momentary loudness uses a 400-millisecond integration window with 75 percent overlap for real-time responsiveness. Short-term loudness averages the last three seconds of momentary values for a smoother reading. Integrated loudness is the average across an entire program, using a gate at -70 LUFS and a floating relative gate 10 LU below the running measurement, and it is the figure used to meet delivery standards. Loudness Range (LRA) describes the range in LU over which most of the loudness sits, capturing dynamic variation. True Peak (dBTP) predicts the actual analog output of a converter by oversampling at four times the original rate, revealing inter-sample peaks that sample-level meters miss; iZotope's True Peak meters are BS.1770-4 compliant, and the guide references ITU-R BS.1770-4 for the technical specification. For distribution, most streaming platforms normalize audio to approximately -14 LUFS integrated loudness, and some services recommend a maximum true peak no greater than -1 or even -2 dBTP to prevent clipping. When mastering, monitoring at normalized loudness against reference tracks helps ensure competitive playback across platforms. For dialogue or podcast work, momentary and short-term readouts help judge the consistency of voices while mixing.

title: First Principles: The Building Blocks of True Knowledge, Farnam Street (fs.blog)
text: First-principles thinking, also called reasoning from first principles, breaks a complex problem down by separating absolute truths from assumptions, then reasoning up from those foundations. It differs fundamentally from reasoning by analogy. As Elon Musk describes it, analogical reasoning means doing something because it is like something else that was already done, whereas the first-principles approach boils things down to the most fundamental truths and reasons up from there. Musk notes that reasoning by analogy is mentally easier, while first-principles thinking demands substantially more effort. The idea traces to classical Western philosophy, originating with Plato and receiving significant contributions from Aristotle and Descartes, thinkers who sought foundational knowledge that holds across domains. Modern practice does not require discovering eternal absolute truths; instead it identifies the elements that are irreducible within a specific context, and that understanding evolves as knowledge expands. Two main techniques help establish first principles. Socratic questioning is a disciplined process that clarifies an idea and its origins, challenges assumptions, looks for evidence, considers alternative viewpoints, examines implications and consequences, and finally questions the original question itself. The Five Whys technique asks why repeatedly until reaching a foundational answer, and it often exposes how little we actually know about something we assumed we understood. Musk's battery example illustrates the payoff: rather than accepting the historical price of about 600 dollars per kilowatt-hour, he broke a battery pack down into its material constituents such as cobalt, nickel, aluminum, carbon, and polymers, priced those materials on the London Metal Exchange, and found the raw material cost was closer to 80 dollars per kilowatt-hour, revealing possibilities that conventional wisdom had obscured.

title: What is Design Thinking?, IDEO U Blog
text: Design thinking is a human-centered approach to innovation that starts from human need. IDEO U frames it as focusing on the people you are creating for, which leads to better products, services, and processes. The method balances three lenses: what is desirable from a human point of view, what is technologically feasible, and what is economically viable, and a solution ideally sits at the intersection of all three. Empathy is foundational: understanding the people you serve deeply before proposing solutions. Rather than a strictly linear recipe, IDEO presents design thinking as a set of iterative phases you move through and revisit. IDEO's framing names seven: Frame a Question (identify a meaningful driving question), Gather Inspiration (discover real needs through observation and immersion in people's lives), Synthesize for Action (find a strategic focus by making sense of what you learned), Generate Ideas (push for many possibilities and breakthrough thinking), Make Ideas Tangible (build quick low-fidelity prototypes to learn), Test to Learn (refine ideas through feedback from real people), and Share the Story (communicate through narrative to inspire action). The process deliberately alternates between two modes of thinking. During ideation, teams practice divergent thinking, going wide, suspending judgment, and embracing wild ideas. During synthesis and selection, they use convergent thinking to spot patterns and extract actionable insights, narrowing broad exploration into strategic focus. This rhythm of expanding then focusing, held together by a human-centered mindset and a bias toward experimentation, is what lets teams tackle ambiguous problems and arrive at solutions people actually want.

title: 7 Simple Rules of Brainstorming, IDEO U Blog
text: IDEO's seven rules of brainstorming come from thousands of sessions across IDEO's teams and client work, and they give a facilitator a framework for unlocking a group's creative potential. The first rule is defer judgment: create a judgment-free zone so people can generate ideas without fear of immediate criticism, which builds the psychological safety needed for contribution. The second rule is encourage wild ideas, on the reasoning that there is often not much difference between outrageous and brilliant, so the extreme ideas open up new territory. The third rule is build on the ideas of others: use and rather than but to extend and combine contributions, keeping energy positive and inclusive rather than shutting suggestions down. The fourth rule is stay focused on the topic, balancing creative divergence against a purposeful aim so the session keeps pointing at the actual challenge. The fifth rule is one conversation at a time, which prevents the group from splintering into side discussions and lets every idea be heard. The sixth rule is be visual: use markers, Post-its, and wall space to externalize thinking so ideas become tangible and shareable in the room. The seventh rule is go for quantity, aiming for a high volume of ideas, roughly 100 ideas in a 60-minute session, because prolific idea generation statistically improves the odds of a breakthrough. Used together, these rules let a facilitator hold divergent, generative energy without letting a session lose focus or momentum.
